fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Shango Is Hercules", "body": "The heart of the episode is David Warner Mathisen's case that Shango, the thunder god of the Yoruba people of Nigeria, is the constellation Hercules. He walks Chance Garton through a 1980 description by the researcher William Bascom, who records that Shango lives in the sky, hurls thunder stones to earth, and spits fire from his mouth. Mathisen matches the carvings point by point to the stars: the flat square head, the full beard, the axe or cudgel, and the tongue lolling out that shows up on Hercules figures worldwide."}, {"title": "A Dance That Copies The Sky", "body": "Mathisen shows photographs of Shango dancers, whose deep lunge, high raised knee, upheld axe and protruding tongue reproduce the outline of Hercules almost exactly. Because many Yoruba were enslaved and taken to Cuba and the Caribbean, those Orisha traditions survive in Santeria, where drummers play rhythms until a dancer manifests a recognizable deity and onlookers say Shango has taken him. For Mathisen this is the whole argument in one image. What is out there in the sky light years away can also come into you, and even our movements reflect the stars."}, {"title": "The Inverted Mortar And Ophiuchus", "body": "Shango's thunder stones are kept on a plate set on an upside down mortar, and initiates get their heads shaved sitting on one. Mathisen asks what an inverted mortar might be in the sky and points to Ophiuchus, directly below Hercules, with the serpent doubling as the pestle. He then tells an African myth in which women pounding grain poke the sky god with their pestles, the heavens recede, and the people stack inverted mortars to climb back up until the tower collapses. Chance jokes it is the book of Jenga. It is the Tower of Babel."}, {"title": "Thunder Gods At Every Latitude", "body": "To show the pattern is global, Mathisen puts up the Maya rain god Chok from a seventh or eighth century vessel in the Met, accession number 1978 412 206, carrying an axe over his back in the unmistakable Hercules posture and grasping a disc where the Northern Crown sits. He traces the four bright stars that form the axe head, notes the same stars become Thor's hammer Mjolnir and the vajra thunderbolt, and identifies the sash ending in a tuft as the trail of stars running off the hip toward Vega. These myths are collected in his nine hundred page Ancient Worldwide System."}, {"title": "Shamanic Gnosis And The Gods Inside You", "body": "Around the star charts runs a larger argument. Quoting Godfrey Higgins and reading Peter Kingsley's book Reality, the two discuss how Parmenides, the supposed father of philosophy, described going to the underworld to meet a goddess, a plainly shamanic account that modern scholars discard. Mathisen notes that sha means to know, so a shaman is one who knows, and that Christian missionaries burned the drums of Scandinavia. Drawing on Michael Hudson on debt forgiveness, Laird Scranton on the Dogon, and Jung, he argues that his newest book, Invoking The Ancient Gods In You, is the real point."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: David Warner Mathisen returns to InnerVerse to teach us about some of the more obscure myths and legends of the world that reflect the astro-theology religion of the ancients. We discuss spiritual context for modern societal turbulence, parallels between shamanism and Gnosticism, star myths as evidence of humanity's transcendental powers, mythological imperialism, the African fire deity Xango, the ritualistic assumption of godly personas, the Mayan thunder god Chaak, and much more.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Stolen Fire and the Termite Mound", "body": "Mathisen opens the members hour with a fire story from the Yarra River valley, preserved in James Frazer's 1930 collection Myths of the Origin of Fire. A woman keeps fire hidden in the tip of her digging stick until a crow tricks her by hiding snakes beneath a termite mound. He reads the mound as Ophiuchus, the snakes as Scorpio beneath it, and the fire as the divine spark in each of us, while Chance adds that the stick matches the staff Ophiuchus sometimes carries. A second tale of two hawk ancestors carrying fire points to Aquila and Cygnus in the Milky Way."}, {"title": "A Rishi, a Princess and One World System", "body": "From India comes Chyavana, a rishi who meditates so long that termites bury him until only his eyes show. A princess mistakes them for glowworms and pokes them out, is promised to him in marriage, and twin healer gods restore his sight and youth in a pool Mathisen links to the Milky Way. All three rise looking identical, which he ties to Ophiuchus with a serpent half on either side. Chance suggests the princess is Sagittarius and notes that renewed youth is serpent symbolism. For Mathisen, a woman poking a termite mound in both India and long isolated Australia is too specific for coincidence."}, {"title": "Reading the Southern Sky", "body": "Living in Australia lets Mathisen show stars that never clear the horizon in North America. He returns to Shango's wife Oya, an antelope who sheds her skin to visit the market until Shango hides it in the rafters, and proposes Centaurus as her animal form, erasing one line so the centaur's torso becomes an antlered head, while admitting he is less sure of her than of Shango as Hercules. He then explains why Orion, the moon and Hercules appear upside down below the equator, using his own photographs, a friend's view of Venus from Tokyo, a Zeppelin metaphor and a Stellarium sky set at 29 degrees south."}, {"title": "Prophecy as Public Theater", "body": "Prompted by Mathisen's Instagram post on stellar rituals, Chance argues that world events are staged to resemble Revelation, citing the quickly healed ear after the 2024 attempt on Donald Trump and the way one man is cast as savior for one side and antichrist for the other. Mathisen thinks of the healed ear at Gethsemane, then draws on his infantry training and a West Point parade for Ronald Reagan to call the unguarded rooftop impossible to overlook. Chance describes left and right trading places on censorship, and Mathisen calls it a deliberate circus run by elites playing a weak hand."}, {"title": "Debt, Credit and a World of Abundance", "body": "Mathisen says the gods of the Odyssey detest suitors who lounge about devouring other people's wealth, and that Midas turning his own daughter to gold shows where endless appetite leads. Chance ties this to debt based currency that sells out the future for instant gratification, a game of musical chairs in which there is never enough money to repay every debt. Mathisen pushes back, pointing to Warren Mosler and modern monetary theory: credit created from nothing is a tool of abundance, the most important public utility, and the real mistake was handing it to Wall Street for private profit. Both agree it works only when those wielding it are moral."}]
